@graph.description: The process chain for an FF&E logistics project. Step 0, scope alignment: the buyer or project team supplies the project address, vendor and purchase-order references when available, FF&E schedule, room matrix, floor plans, installation drawings, storage interval, access rules, and the boundary between logistics support and licensed or technical work; the full scope is reviewed and quoted at one flat rate. Step 1, purchase-order receiving: staggered vendor shipments are received as one project stream rather than unrelated freight. Step 2, dock inventory and condition: freight is counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock, tied to project and purchase-order references where supplied, and labeled and inventory-tagged to its room or phase destination, with visible damage, shortages, overages, and discrepancies recorded as receiving exceptions while the delivery record is fresh. Step 3, warehousing: received product is held in leased space — furniture-padded or shrink-wrapped as the item requires, with corner and edge protectors on finished surfaces — under the company's published storage basis — 30-day minimum, customer access, pricing per job, monthly, or by volume — until the building sequence calls for it. Step 4, sequence and pull: product is pulled by model room, floor, room number, department, classroom, office, or phase, not by the order in which vendor trucks arrived. Step 5, site delivery: the sequence moves to the site around dock and elevator reservations, active trades, protected routes, and occupied areas. Step 6, installation support: crews unpack, assemble, place, and level FF&E within the logistics scope — working with furniture pads under pieces in motion and corner protectors on finished edges — and set in place items that do not require licensed-trade connection or manufacturer commissioning. Step 7, packaging and debris removal: packaging generated by the delivered FF&E is removed within the project scope. Step 8, punch and opening readiness: completed areas, outstanding items, and exceptions are walked and documented so the project team can see what is finished and what remains open. Domain reference (Bailey's Workplace FF&E guide, labeled as such): mature programs often coordinate delivery through a tentative window several weeks out, a firmer confirmation seven to ten days out, and a final confirmation 72 hours ahead; the company's project gates are set in the written scope with the GC or project team, not promised as universal lead times.

@graph.description: Taxonomy for FF&E logistics. Hospitality: new hotels and resorts, hotel renovations and property-improvement projects, model rooms, guest rooms by floor and room number, lobbies, restaurants, meeting and event spaces, and back-of-house areas; the controlling pressure is a fixed opening or reopening date and room-by-room completion. Healthcare and senior living: hospital expansions and renovations, clinics and medical offices, rehabilitation and support spaces, and senior-living openings or renovations; the sequence unit is the department, suite, wing, resident area, or phase, and facility, manufacturer, biomedical, and licensed teams retain clinical and technical work. Office and commercial: corporate fit-outs, consolidations, restacks, workstations and systems furniture, private offices, conference and training rooms, restaurants, retail, and back-of-house spaces; the sequence unit is the floor, neighborhood, workstation group, dining zone, or department. Education: classroom buildings, lecture and seminar spaces, libraries, student housing, administrative offices, and student-life areas; the sequence follows the academic calendar and building, floor, classroom, or residence unit. Item classes include casegoods, beds and seating, tables, workstations and systems furniture, storage pieces, artwork and mirrors, lighting fixtures for placement only, and equipment for set-in-place support only where no licensed connection, calibration, activation, or commissioning is required. OS&E is a distinct node in this taxonomy: operating supplies and consumables are not FF&E and are not automatically included in the FF&E logistics scope.

@graph.description: Compliance and boundaries for FF&E logistics. Site control: project-specific access, security, dock, elevator, occupancy, and facility rules are confirmed before dispatch; no blanket clearance, screening, certification, insurance, bonding, or facility-credential claim is published. Materials handling (domain reference): OSHA 29 CFR 1910.176 addresses safe clearances, clear and marked aisles, secure storage, stable stacking, and housekeeping; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.178 governs powered industrial trucks as a regulated equipment class. No equipment list, forklift claim, or operator credential is published for this service — equipment varies by project and is confirmed in the scope. Installation boundary: the logistics scope covers unpacking, furniture assembly, placement, leveling, and set-in-place support. Electrical wiring and connections, plumbing and gas connections, fire-protection and life-safety work, structural alteration or regulated anchoring, manufacturer activation, calibration, certification, commissioning, clinical validation, network activation, and warranty repair remain with the licensed trade, manufacturer, facility team, or installer of record. Healthcare boundary: FF&E logistics in a hospital, clinic, or senior-living setting is physical receiving, warehousing, delivery, and placement support under the facility's protocols; it is not a clinical service and carries no HIPAA, infection-control certification, medical-device, or patient-care claim. Commercial boundary: no FF&E procurement, design, purchasing, specification, project count, client, testimonial, on-time record, damage record, insurance limit, valuation program, owned warehouse, dedicated FF&E warehouse, climate-controlled storage, real-time inventory portal, or nationwide FF&E coverage is claimed.
